analogy.p: Imagine a Ferris wheel of radius 1 turning steadily, with you at the 3 o'clock position when the angle is 0°. Your **height above the centre** as the wheel turns through the angle x is **sin x**: it starts at 0, reaches 1 at the top (90°), returns to 0 at 9 o'clock (180°), reaches −1 at the bottom (270°) and repeats each turn. Your **horizontal distance from the centre** is **cos x**: it starts at 1 (the 3 o'clock point), is 0 at the top and bottom, and −1 at 9 o'clock. Tan x is the **steepness of the line from the centre to you**, which becomes infinitely steep at the top and bottom, which is why tan has asymptotes at 90° and 270°. The analogy breaks down because a real Ferris wheel stops, and the graphs of sin, cos and tan carry on for ever in both directions with perfect repetition.
analogy.t: A Ferris wheel and its shadow

bullets: **sin x** and **cos x** both repeat every **360°** and always lie between **−1 and 1**.
**tan x** repeats every **180°**, can take **any** value, and is **undefined** at 90° and 270°.
The graphs let you **read off values**, such as sin 210° or cos 300°, without a calculator, using symmetry.
A calculator gives only **one** answer when you use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹; the graph shows you where the **other** solutions are.
Your calculator must be in **degree mode** (look for a D on the display) for all of these questions.
You must know the **exact values** for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° (and tan up to 60°), usually in a non-calculator paper.
Trig graphs link to transformations of graphs (stretches, shifts and reflections) and to the sine and cosine rules.
Examiners test this topic through sketching questions, 'solve for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360' questions and matching a graph to its equation.
core.h: What the specification asks and why trig graphs matter
core.p: For Edexcel Higher you must **recognise, sketch and interpret the graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x** for angles of any size (in degrees), know their key features, and use the graphs and symmetry to find **all** the solutions of simple trigonometric equations in a given range, usually 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. You also need the **exact values** of sin, cos and tan for the special angles. Until now, trig has meant lengths and angles in right-angled triangles, where angles are between 0° and 90°. The graphs extend the idea to **any** angle, showing that sine, cosine and tangent are repeating (periodic) functions, and they explain why an equation such as sin x = 0.5 has more than one answer.

bullets: The **period** is **360°**: sin(x + 360°) = sin x, so the graph repeats every 360°. For example sin 400° = sin 40°.
The **amplitude** is **1** and the **range** is **−1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1**. Sine can never equal 2 or −1.5.
The **roots** (zeros) are at x = 0°, 180°, 360° (and every multiple of 180° outside this range).
The graph is **symmetrical about x = 90° and x = 270°**: sin(180° − x) = sin x, which is why sin 30° = sin 150° = 0.5.
It has **rotational symmetry** about (180°, 0) and about the origin: sin(−x) = −sin x, so sin(−30°) = −0.5.
Between 0° and 180° sine is **positive**; between 180° and 360° sine is **negative**.
Always draw it as a **smooth wave** with rounded peaks and troughs, never with straight lines or sharp points.
core.h: The sine graph y = sin x
core.p: The sine graph is a smooth, repeating wave. It starts at the origin (0, 0), rises to a **maximum of 1 at x = 90°**, falls through zero at **180°**, reaches a **minimum of −1 at x = 270°**, and returns to zero at **360°**. This pattern is one **cycle** and then repeats exactly. The size of the wave, from the middle to the peak, is the **amplitude**, which is 1 for y = sin x.

bullets: The **period** is **360°** and the **amplitude** is **1**; the range is again −1 ≤ cos x ≤ 1.
The **roots** are at **x = 90° and x = 270°** (and 90° + any multiple of 180°).
The graph is **symmetrical about x = 180°**: cos(360° − x) = cos x, so cos 60° = cos 300° = 0.5.
It is also symmetrical about the y-axis: **cos(−x) = cos x**, so cos(−60°) = 0.5.
Cosine is **positive** from 0° to 90° and from 270° to 360°, and **negative** between 90° and 270°.
Another useful link: cos x = sin(90° − x), so cos 30° = sin 60° = √3/2.
The only difference between the sine and cosine graphs is **where they start**: sine starts at (0, 0), cosine starts at (0, 1).
core.h: The cosine graph y = cos x
core.p: The cosine graph has exactly the same wave shape as sine, but it starts at the **top** instead of the middle. It begins at **(0°, 1)**, falls through zero at **90°**, reaches a **minimum of −1 at 180°**, rises through zero at **270°** and returns to **1 at 360°**. Cosine is the sine graph shifted **90° to the left**, which is why cos x = sin(x + 90°).

bullets: The **period is 180°**, not 360°: tan(x + 180°) = tan x, so tan 225° = tan 45° = 1.
The **asymptotes** at x = 90° and x = 270° are drawn as **dashed lines** and the curve never touches or crosses them.
The **roots** are at x = 0°, 180° and 360°.
The graph has **no maximum or minimum** and the range is **all real numbers**: tan x can equal any value, including 100 or −1000.
**Tan is positive** in 0°–90° and 180°–270°, and **negative** in 90°–180° and 270°–360°.
Near an asymptote the curve gets steeper and steeper; tan 89° ≈ 57.3 and tan 89.9° ≈ 573.
tan x = sin x ÷ cos x explains the whole shape: zeros of sine give zeros of tan, zeros of cosine give asymptotes.
core.h: The tangent graph y = tan x
core.p: The tangent graph looks completely different: it is made of **repeating branches** separated by vertical **asymptotes**. For 0° to 360° the asymptotes are at **x = 90°** and **x = 270°**. Because tan x = sin x ÷ cos x, tangent is undefined whenever cos x = 0, that is at 90°, 270° and so on, and the graph shoots off to very large positive or negative values near those lines. Each branch rises steadily from left to right.

bullets: **sin x:** period 360°, starts at 0, max at 90°, min at 270°, zeros at 0°, 180°, 360°.
**cos x:** period 360°, starts at 1, max at 0° and 360°, min at 180°, zeros at 90° and 270°.
**tan x:** period 180°, starts at 0, asymptotes at 90° and 270°, zeros at 0°, 180°, 360°.
**Sine mirror:** sin(180° − x) = sin x. **Cosine mirror:** cos(360° − x) = cos x. **Tangent repeat:** tan(x + 180°) = tan x.
**Negative angles:** sin(−x) = −sin x, cos(−x) = cos x, tan(−x) = −tan x.
**Shifting 180°:** sin(180° + x) = −sin x, cos(180° + x) = −cos x, tan(180° + x) = tan x.
**Link:** cos x = sin(x + 90°) and sin x = cos(x − 90°); both graphs are the same wave shifted by 90°.
Quick check on any answer: positive/negative must match the graph in that region.
core.h: Comparing the three graphs and the key symmetries
core.p: It is much easier to remember the graphs as a family than as separate facts. Sine and cosine are identical waves in different positions, and tangent comes from dividing one by the other. The symmetries of the graphs are the key to finding **second solutions** without a calculator and to finding angles outside 0° to 90°.

bullets: **cos:** 0° → 1, 30° → √3/2, 45° → √2/2, 60° → 1/2, 90° → 0. The cos row is the sin row in reverse.
From the 45° triangle (1, 1, √2): sin 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2 after rationalising, and tan 45° = 1/1 = 1.
From the 30°–60°–90° triangle (1, √3, 2): the side opposite 30° is 1, opposite 60° is √3, hypotenuse 2, so sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3 = √3/3.
Check: tan = sin ÷ cos. For 60°: (√3/2) ÷ (1/2) = √3 ✓.
Use these values together with the graph symmetries to find exact values of angles such as sin 150° (= sin 30° = 1/2) and cos 120° (= −cos 60° = −1/2).
core.h: Exact values of sin, cos and tan
core.p: You must know the exact values for the special angles without a calculator. They come from two triangles: a **right-angled isosceles triangle** (half a square) with sides 1, 1, √2 for 45°, and **half an equilateral triangle** with sides 1, √3, 2 for 30° and 60°. Use **sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent (SOH CAH TOA)** to read off the ratios. Drawing the triangle in an exam is the safest way to recover a forgotten value.

bullets: **Positive k:** the answers are in the first two quadrants: x = sin⁻¹ k and x = 180° − sin⁻¹ k. Example: sin x = 0.5 gives x = **30°** and **150°**.
**Negative k:** the calculator gives a negative angle (sin⁻¹(−0.5) = −30°), which is outside the range. Use the **related angle** 30°: the answers are **180° + 30° = 210°** and **360° − 30° = 330°**.
**k = 1:** only one solution, x = 90°, where the line touches the peak. **k = −1:** only x = 270°.
**|k| > 1:** **no solutions**, because sine is never larger than 1 or smaller than −1.
**k = 0:** solutions at 0°, 180° and 360° (three in the range 0° to 360° inclusive).
If the equation is not yet in the form sin x = k, **rearrange** first: 2 sin x = 1 becomes sin x = 0.5; 3 sin x + 1 = 0 becomes sin x = −1/3.
Check each answer by putting it back in your calculator, and check that both are inside the stated range.
core.h: Solving sin x = k using the graph and symmetry
core.p: To solve **sin x = k** for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, find the first answer with sin⁻¹ k on your calculator, then use the symmetry of the sine graph about x = 90° to find the second: **x = 180° − first answer**. Graphically, you draw the horizontal line y = k and read off where it meets the wave; because the wave goes up and down once in each cycle, there are **two** intersections for any k strictly between −1 and 1. The reason for two answers is the mirror symmetry of the wave about its peak.

bullets: **cos x = −0.5:** cos⁻¹(−0.5) = **120°** (the calculator gives this directly), and 360° − 120° = **240°**. So x = 120° or 240°.
**tan x = −1:** the calculator gives −45°. Add **180°** to get 135°, and add **360°** to get 315°. So x = 135° or 315°.
For cos x = k the solutions always sit **symmetrically about 180°** (for example 120° and 240°); for tan the solutions are exactly **180° apart**.
The cos x = ±1 cases give a single solution (0° or 360° for 1, 180° for −1), and tan x = k always has two solutions in 0° to 360°.
core.h: Solving cos x = k and tan x = k
core.p: The same approach works for cosine and tangent, but the symmetry is different, so the second solution is found differently. For **cos x = k**, use the symmetry of the cosine graph about x = 180°: the second solution is **360° − first answer**. For **tan x = k**, the graph repeats every 180°, so the second solution is **first answer + 180°**. Always draw a quick sketch of the graph with the line y = k to see how many solutions you expect.

bullets: Step 1: rearrange to sin x = k, cos x = k or tan x = k.
Step 2: find the related acute angle α = inverse function of |k| (ignore any minus sign).
Step 3: decide which quadrants have the right sign: sin + in quadrants 1 and 2; cos + in quadrants 1 and 4; tan + in quadrants 1 and 3 (and negative in the others).
Step 4: write the angles: quadrant 1: α; quadrant 2: 180° − α; quadrant 3: 180° + α; quadrant 4: 360° − α.
Example: sin x = −0.5. α = 30°. Sine is negative in quadrants 3 and 4: x = 180° + 30° = **210°** and x = 360° − 30° = **330°**.
Example: cos x = −0.5. α = 60°. Cosine is negative in quadrants 2 and 3: x = 180° − 60° = **120°** and x = 180° + 60° = **240°**.
Example: tan x = −1. α = 45°. Tangent is negative in quadrants 2 and 4: x = 180° − 45° = **135°** and x = 360° − 45° = **315°**.
The CAST method is equivalent to the graph methods above; use whichever you remember best, but be consistent and always check with a sketch.
core.h: A reliable method: the related angle and the CAST diagram
core.p: The **CAST diagram** (or 'All Sin Tan Cos') shows which of sin, cos and tan are positive in each quadrant when you go anticlockwise from 0°. In the first quadrant (0° to 90°) **All** are positive; in the second (90° to 180°) only **Sin**; in the third (180° to 270°) only **Tan**; and in the fourth (270° to 360°) only **Cos**. To solve an equation, find the **related (acute) angle** by ignoring the sign of k, then use the quadrants where the sign matches to place the angle.

bullets: **tan(x ± 180°) = tan x**, so tan 405° = tan 45° = 1.
**Negative angles** go clockwise: add 360° to reduce them. sin(−30°) = sin 330° = −0.5; cos(−60°) = cos 300° = 0.5.
If the range is wider, for example −360° ≤ x ≤ 360°, find the solutions in 0° to 360°, then subtract 360° from each to get the solutions in −360° to 0°.
The shape of the graph for any interval is the same wave repeated: extend the sketch to the left and right.
In real life, periodic functions describe tides, sound waves, alternating current and the height of a point on a Ferris wheel.
Questions about repeating patterns, such as 'a wheel turns every 12 s', use the same idea of a period.
core.h: Angles of any size and periodic behaviour
core.p: Because the graphs repeat, trig functions are defined for **any** angle, including angles larger than 360° and negative angles. Adding or subtracting a full turn does not change sine or cosine, and adding or subtracting half a turn does not change tangent. This explains why a calculator can give sin 750° and why an equation can have infinitely many solutions if no range is given. Questions at GCSE nearly always give a range, so you list the solutions inside it.

bullets: **y = a sin x:** the amplitude becomes |a|, the maximum is a and the minimum is −a; the period stays 360°. For y = 3 sin x the maximum is 3 at 90°.
**y = sin x + c:** the whole graph moves **up c units**; the centre line is y = c and the range is c − 1 ≤ y ≤ c + 1.
**y = sin bx** (or cos bx): the period becomes **360° ÷ b**. y = sin 2x repeats every 180° and completes **two** full cycles in 0° to 360°.
**y = −sin x:** reflection in the x-axis. It starts at 0 and goes **down** first, reaching −1 at 90°.
**y = sin(x − 90°)** (shift right by 90°) = −cos x; **y = sin(x + 90°)** (shift left by 90°) = cos x; **y = cos(x − 90°)** = sin x.
**y = tan 2x:** period 90°, with asymptotes at 45°, 135°, 225° and 315°.
To sketch a transformed graph: transform the key points (the max, min and zero points) and join them smoothly.
core.p: The transformations of graphs you meet elsewhere apply directly to sin, cos and tan. Multiplying outside the function stretches the wave vertically, multiplying inside changes how fast it repeats, and adding shifts it. Knowing a few standard results lets you sketch or match graphs quickly, using the key points of the basic graph and moving them.

bullets: **Maximum and minimum** give the amplitude and the vertical position: if the graph oscillates between −3 and 3 it is a 3 × sin or 3 × cos graph.
**Period:** measure from one peak to the next peak. If peaks are 180° apart, b = 360° ÷ 180° = 2.
**Starting point:** starting at 0 and rising = sin; starting at the maximum = cos; starting at 0 with asymptotes = tan.
To **read a value** (for example sin 200°) go to 200° on the x-axis, go up to the curve and read across to the y-axis: about −0.34.
To **solve an equation from a graph** draw the horizontal line y = k with a ruler, mark the intersections and read down to the x-axis.
In a context question, say what the feature means: 'The maximum height of the tide is 3 m' or 'the temperature repeats every 12 months'.
Check your equation by testing one point from the graph.
If asked for 'all solutions between 0° and 360°', **count the intersections** shown on the graph to make sure you have not missed any.
core.p: In an exam you might be given a drawn trig graph and asked to read values, find the equation, or explain what a feature means. The skill is to look at the **maximum, minimum, period and starting point** and to match them to the standard forms. Use the scale carefully: the x-axis is usually in steps of 30° or 90°, and the y-axis shows the range of values.

bullets: **Right-angled triangle trigonometry** (SOH CAH TOA) is the starting point; the exact values come from the same ratios.
**Sine rule, cosine rule and area = ½ab sin C:** these use sin and cos for angles above 90° (an obtuse C), and the graph reminds you sin(180° − x) = sin x, so sin C is positive.
**Transformations of graphs:** y = f(x) + a, y = f(x + a), y = af(x) and y = f(ax) all work on trig graphs.
**Solving equations:** rearranging 3 sin x − 1 = 0 uses algebra first, then trig.
**Vectors and bearings** use angles of any size and sine/cosine of angles between 0° and 360°.
**Surds:** exact values often need rationalising, for example 1/√2 = √2/2.
**Circle theorems and 3D trigonometry** use the same ratios in more complex diagrams.
**Calculator skills:** check degree mode and use the inverse functions correctly.
core.p: Trig graphs connect with several other parts of the Higher course. Seeing these links helps you plan multi-step solutions and avoid mistakes, because several different questions ask the same underlying thing in different disguises.

exam: **Command words:** *Sketch* = correct shape with key points labelled (not to scale); *Solve* = find all the values in the range; *Write down* = no working needed; *Show that* = prove the stated result with exact values.

**Sketch questions (2 to 3 marks):** draw at least one full cycle on the stated range with scale marks at 90° steps, mark the key points (for example (90°, 1) and (270°, −1)), and draw a smooth curve.

**Solve sin x = k, 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° (3 marks):** M1 for sin⁻¹ k (or correct related angle), A1 for the first angle, A1 for the second (usually 180° − first). A solution with one angle only scores 2 marks.
**Rearranging first:** for 2 sin x + 1 = 0, M1 for sin x = −0.5, then 210° and 330°; show the rearranged equation clearly.

**Exact values (non-calculator):** write the surd form; do not give decimals. Use the triangle to show where a value comes from if you cannot recall it. A decimal approximation usually scores no marks.
**Reading graphs:** draw a ruled horizontal line at y = k and mark where it meets the curve; give answers within the tolerance (for example ±5°).
**Match the graph:** check period, maximum/minimum and the starting point. State the equation, for example y = 2 sin x or y = cos 2x, and give the reason.
**Graph questions with asymptotes:** draw dashed lines at x = 90° and x = 270° for tan and say 'asymptote' if asked what happens there.
**Use symmetry reasoning in words:** 'sin is symmetrical about 90°, so sin 150° = sin 30°' scores a mark for the reason.
**Checks:** the range of sin and cos is −1 to 1, so an answer such as sin x = 1.4 means 'no solutions'; check your calculator is in degrees.
**Marks for working:** write the line sin⁻¹(...) = so the examiner can award method marks even if the arithmetic slips.

mistakes.r: Check the calculator is in **degrees** (D). Test by typing sin 30: the answer must be 0.5.
mistakes.w: Using a calculator in radians (or gradians) mode, so sin 30° does not give 0.5.

mistakes.r: For 0° to 360° a sin or cos equation (with |k| < 1) has **two** solutions: use the graph symmetry or CAST to find the second.
mistakes.w: Giving only the calculator answer for sin x = 0.5 and missing 150°.

mistakes.r: For tan the second solution is **x + 180°**, because the tan graph repeats every 180°.
mistakes.w: For tan x = k, using 180° − x as the second answer.

mistakes.r: Use the related angle: x = **210° and 330°**; the answer must lie inside the stated range.
mistakes.w: Leaving a negative angle such as −30° as the answer to sin x = −0.5.

mistakes.r: **Sine** starts at (0, 0); **cosine** starts at (0, 1). Label the key points to show which is which.
mistakes.w: Drawing the cosine graph starting at the origin, or the sine graph starting at 1.

mistakes.r: The tan graph has **no max/min**, rises in each branch, and approaches the **dashed asymptotes** at 90° and 270° without touching them.
mistakes.w: Sketching the tan graph with a maximum and minimum, or crossing the asymptotes.

mistakes.r: The period of tan is **180°**; sin and cos have period 360°.
mistakes.w: Stating that tan has a period of 360°.

mistakes.r: Use the triangles: sin 30° = 1/2 (opposite the smallest angle is the shortest side), sin 60° = √3/2.
mistakes.w: Mixing up exact values, for example sin 30° = √3/2.

mistakes.r: Draw a **smooth curve** with rounded peaks and troughs, symmetrical about each turning point.
mistakes.w: Drawing the wave with straight lines or sharp peaks.

mistakes.r: cos x = −0.5 gives **120° and 240°** (cosine is negative in quadrants 2 and 3); 60° and 300° belong to cos x = +0.5.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong direction for a negative k with cosine (for example giving 60° and 300° for cos x = −0.5).

summary: The specification asks you to recognise, sketch and interpret the graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x for angles of any size in degrees, to know their key features (period, amplitude, roots, asymptotes), to know the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and to use the graphs and symmetry to find all solutions of trigonometric equations in a given range. It matters because trig graphs explain why equations like sin x = 0.5 have several answers and they appear regularly in Higher sketching and solving questions.

terms.d: A function whose graph repeats exactly after a fixed interval, called the period.
The length of one complete cycle of a periodic graph: 360° for sin and cos, 180° for tan.
The distance from the middle (centre line) of a wave to its maximum; 1 for y = sin x and y = cos x.
One complete repeat of the wave pattern of a periodic function.
In a right-angled triangle, opposite ÷ hypotenuse; as a graph, y = sin x, a wave starting at (0°, 0).
In a right-angled triangle, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse; as a graph, y = cos x, a wave starting at (0°, 1).
In a right-angled triangle, opposite ÷ adjacent; also sin x ÷ cos x; the graph has asymptotes at 90° and 270°.
A line that a curve gets closer and closer to but never touches; the tan graph has vertical asymptotes.
The button on a calculator that finds the angle from a ratio; it gives only one value.
The single angle the calculator gives for an inverse trig function.
The acute angle found by ignoring the sign of k, used to find other solutions in other quadrants.
One of the four sections of a full turn: 0°–90°, 90°–180°, 180°–270°, 270°–360°.
A memory aid showing which of cos, sin and tan are positive in each quadrant (All, Sin, Tan, Cos).
A value left in surd or fraction form, such as √3/2, instead of a rounded decimal.
The set of y-values a function can take: −1 ≤ y ≤ 1 for sin and cos; all values for tan.
A change to a graph, such as a stretch, reflection or translation.

worked.q: Solve (a) 2 sin x = 1 and (b) cos x = −0.5, for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. (5 marks)
steps: The sine graph is symmetrical about 90°, so the second solution is 180° − 30° = 150° (A1).
The cosine graph is symmetrical about 180°, so the second solution is 360° − 120° = 240° (A1).
Check both answers by drawing the horizontal lines y = 0.5 and y = −0.5 on a sketch: each meets the wave twice in 0° to 360°.

worked.q: Given that sin 40° = 0.643 (3 d.p.), write down (a) another angle between 0° and 180° with sine 0.643, (b) all angles between 0° and 360° with sin x = −0.643, (c) a value of x between 0° and 90° with cos x = 0.643. (5 marks)
steps: (a) sin(180° − x) = sin x, so the other angle is 180° − 40° = 140° (B1).
(b) sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, using the related angle 40°: 180° + 40° = 220° and 360° − 40° = 320° (B1, B1).
(c) cos x = sin(90° − x), so cos 50° = sin 40° = 0.643 and x = 50° (B1, B1 for the reason).

worked.ans: (a) maximum 3, minimum −3, period 360°; (b) period 180°, roots at 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°; (c) 1.
worked.q: (a) Write down the maximum value, the minimum value and the period of y = 3 cos x. (b) Describe the graph of y = cos 2x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° (period and where it crosses the x-axis). (c) Without a calculator, work out the exact value of 2 sin 60° × tan 30°. (6 marks)
steps: (a) The amplitude is 3, so the maximum is 3 and the minimum is −3; the period is unchanged at 360° (B1, B1).

(b) y = cos bx has period 360° ÷ b. With b = 2 the period is 180°, so there are two full cycles in 0° to 360° (M1). It starts at (0°, 1), crosses the x-axis at 45°, 135°, 225° and 315°, and has minimum points at 90° and 270° (A1).
